Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Public Transport: Bus riding, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Vignette:
Dolores is a 69-year-old married woman of North American descent who has worked the agricultural fields of California's Central Valley for most of her adult life. She presented for treatment following a sexual assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago, and her PCL-5 score of 67 places her symptoms in a severe range. What brought her finally to the clinic door was not a single breaking point but a slow accumulation — the sense that her world had shrunk to something she no longer recognized as a life.

The assault took place on a late afternoon in early autumn. Dolores had finished a shift and boarded a rural transit bus for the forty-minute ride home, as she had done hundreds of times before. The bus was nearly empty. A man she did not know sat beside her, and before she could fully register what was happening, he had assaulted her in the back of that near-deserted vehicle. She did not scream. She has never been fully able to explain to herself why she did not scream, and that silence has become one of the heaviest things she carries. When the bus reached her stop she walked home, told no one, and went to bed.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not stay where she tried to put it. It arrived without warning — while she was bent over a row of crops, while she was washing dishes, while her husband was speaking to her about something ordinary. The memory did not announce itself; it simply appeared, sudden and complete, pulling her back into the particular quality of light on that bus, the smell of the vinyl seat. Her husband noticed she had become distant but did not press her, and she offered nothing. She had come to believe, in a way she could not quite articulate but felt with certainty, that she was somehow permanently altered — that the woman who had boarded that bus and the woman who got off it were not the same person, and that no one around her could understand what that meant.

She stopped taking the bus entirely. This had concrete consequences: the fields where she works are accessible by bus or by a ride she must ask others for, and asking felt unbearable. She began arriving late or missing days, and her supervisor had spoken to her twice about her reliability. She said nothing to explain herself. She had also begun avoiding the social rhythms that had once structured her days — the small conversations between rows, the shared lunches, the neighborly talk at the end of a shift. Certain topics, she had learned, could pull the memory forward without warning: anything touching on being alone, on men, on buses, on not being believed. She could not predict exactly when a conversation would turn that way, so she found it safer to be absent from conversations altogether.

At home, Dolores drinks in the evenings. She does not call it a problem; she calls it the only time her body feels quiet. She has also developed a habit of mentally walking herself through every possible way a situation could go wrong before she enters it — rehearsing the worst so that, she reasons, she will not be caught off guard again. She checks behind her when she walks, particularly in the fields and in parking areas, scanning for anyone approaching from behind. She feels safe only in her own kitchen and, on good days, in a particular corner of the field where she can see in all directions. Everywhere else, her body remains on alert.

What frightens her most is not the memory itself but what she has concluded about herself because of it: that she cannot trust her own judgment, that she failed herself at the moment it mattered most, that she is now somehow outside the ordinary human community — an outsider to her own marriage, to her coworkers, to the life she lived before. She feels isolated in a way that feels permanent rather than circumstantial, as though a wall has been built that she did not build and cannot dismantle.

She came to the clinic because her husband told her he was scared for her, and because some part of her — quiet, persistent — is not yet willing to accept that this is simply who she is now.
